cues.text: Every time a company scans its code for security flaws,
developers get buried in alerts
953 across just 10 open-source projects.
Most are false alarms, so people stop reading,
and real vulnerabilities slip through.
AI could help — but for banks, hospitals and manufacturers,
uploading private source code to a cloud AI is not an option.
This is NetLens:
an AI security gateway that runs entirely on-premises
on Intel hardware, powered by OpenVINO.
NetLens works in two stages.
First, Semgrep rules sweep the entire codebase and flag anything that might be dangerous
fast and thorough, but noisy.
Then every flagged function goes to our fine-tuned CodeBERT model,
which actually reads the code and decides:
real vulnerability, or false alarm?
Here it is on healthchecks,
a real open-source project of 21,000 lines.
51 alerts go in;
37 are thrown out as noise.
Across 10 projects and 640,000 lines,
the alerts a developer has to read drop by 84%.
To run on-premises, NetLens must be fast on hardware companies already own.
So we converted our model to OpenVINO and quantized it to INT8
8-bit integers instead of 32-bit floats.
Same model, same 152 functions, three engines:
PyTorch on the CPU, OpenVINO INT8 on the same Intel CPU,
and OpenVINO on the Intel integrated GPU — watch its load climb in real time.
When both OpenVINO engines finish, PyTorch is still less than halfway.
In our benchmarks, that's nearly 4× the throughput on the same chip
and the GPU keeps the CPU free for Semgrep.
Finding a vulnerability is only half the job.
So on the same Intel GPU, NetLens runs a local code model,
Qwen2.5-Coder, compressed to 4 bits.
It explains how an attacker would exploit the bug,
then writes the patch — a SQL injection becomes a parameterized query.
About 15 tokens per second on laptop integrated graphics
and 0 bytes of source code leave the machine.
Quantization makes the model 4× smaller — with no loss in accuracy:
macro-F1 is identical to the third decimal place across 2,742 test functions.
And on an Intel Arc Pro B70,
we project 3–5 milliseconds per function
10,000 findings reviewed in under half a minute.
Semgrep on the CPU.
CodeBERT and the fix-writing model sharing a single 32 GB Arc Pro B70.
The whole pipeline, in a single ASUS workstation.
Your code never leaves.
Your vulnerabilities do.
